reference.source: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A tumour of Schwann cell (neural) origin, despite the obsolete term myoblastoma, confirmed by strong S100 and SOX10 positivity
The tongue is the single commonest site, followed by skin, subcutis, breast, and the gastrointestinal tract
It presents as a small, firm, painless nodule and is more frequent in adults, in women, and in people of African ancestry
The tumour cells have abundant eosinophilic granular cytoplasm packed with lysosomes that are periodic acid-Schiff positive and diastase resistant
Pustulo-ovoid bodies of Milian are a helpful cytological clue
Overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia can be mistaken for a well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma on a superficial biopsy
The great majority are benign; a rare malignant variant is defined by features such as large size, necrosis, high mitotic activity, and pleomorphism
Conservative complete local excision is the treatment of choice
reference.pathophysiology: Granular cell tumour is a neoplasm of Schwann cell derivation, a lineage established by consistent expression of S100 protein and SOX10 and by ultrastructural findings of abundant autophagic lysosomes. These accumulated lysosomes give the tumour cells their characteristic granular eosinophilic cytoplasm and their strong periodic acid-Schiff positivity that resists diastase digestion. The cells infiltrate between collagen bundles and around nerves and adnexal structures, which explains why margins can be difficult to assess. When the lesion lies immediately beneath a mucosal or epidermal surface it frequently induces marked pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of the overlying epithelium, a reactive change that closely simulates invasive squamous carcinoma and is a well-recognised source of diagnostic error. Malignant examples are rare and are defined by a constellation of adverse histological features rather than by a single criterion.
additionalDifferentials: Well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, mimicked by overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia
Rhabdomyoma and other granular cell lesions
Schwannoma and other peripheral nerve sheath tumours
additionalInvestigations: Excisional or incisional biopsy with histological assessment
Immunohistochemistry for S100 and SOX10 to confirm Schwann cell origin
Periodic acid-Schiff staining with diastase to demonstrate granules
Careful pathological review to avoid overcalling overlying epithelial hyperplasia as carcinoma
Imaging of the lesion and, for deep or large tumours, of regional structures
Assessment against malignancy criteria when clinical or histological features are worrying
redFlags: Rapid growth, large size, or a deep-seated location
Ulceration, necrosis, or fixation suggesting a malignant variant
Regional lymphadenopathy or evidence of metastasis
reference.prognosis: Most granular cell tumours are benign and are cured by complete excision, with recurrence usually reflecting incomplete removal. The uncommon malignant variant behaves aggressively with a substantial risk of metastasis and a correspondingly poorer outcome.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing overlying pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia as squamous cell carcinoma and undertaking unnecessarily radical surgery
Assuming all lesions are benign and overlooking the histological criteria for malignancy
Incomplete excision due to the infiltrative, poorly demarcated margins
Retaining the outdated myoblastoma label and misattributing a muscle origin
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
